Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue

Thursday, November 5, 2026 · 6:00 – 10:00 pm · Online420-1C2-DW Threats and Risks · AEC (Attestation d'études collégiales) Cybersecurity: Prevention and Intervention (LEA.D8)Topic 3 — Identifying Threats (Part 2)Competency EZ02 — element 2 (criterion 2.3: methodical analysis of public information sources)Hour 1 — lecture in four lessons (60 min) · Lab 1 due tonight · Lab 2 starts in hour 2Student hand-out

Good evening. On Monday you learned who the threat actors are and how they work: cybercriminals, hacktivists, state-sponsored groups, opportunistic attackers, and the three kinds of insiders. Tonight you learn where the profession reads about them every week, how to read those documents without being misled, and how to turn the reading into the second chapter of your Integrative Project: Kalmia's threat catalogue.

Four lessons in one hour. Lesson 1: the public sources — alerts, advisories, newsletters, reports — and the weekly routine that keeps a small company informed. Lesson 2: the two identifier systems the whole industry shares, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) for vulnerabilities and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) for attacker behaviours, with the three scores that say how urgent a vulnerability is. Lesson 3: the seven-question method for reading and rating any threat report, with the two six-level scales, the estimative words of the Cyber Centre and the TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) markings. Lesson 4: how the catalogue is built, column by column, and checked. Lab 1 is due tonight at midnight; Lab 2 starts in hour 2 with the rows we build together.

The one fact to remember

Public sources are read against your own inventory. A Critical vulnerability in a product you do not run is somebody else's problem; a High vulnerability on your Internet-facing web shop with a KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) entry is tonight's problem. Severity is a property of the flaw; relevance is a property of your organization; evidence is what connects them — and every row of the threat catalogue must carry all three.

By the end of this hour you will be able to

  1. Name the six families of public threat-information sources, distinguish an alert, an advisory and a newsletter, and run the four-step weekly watch routine against the Lab 1 inventory.
  2. Read a CVE record and an ATT&CK page, keep CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (severity), EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (probability) and KEV (evidence) apart, and write a threat event with both identifiers.
  3. Apply the seven questions to any threat report, rate the source (A–F) and the information (1–6), respect TLP 2.0, use the Cyber Centre's estimative language correctly and record a decision with its reasons.
  4. Build and check a threat catalogue in the fifteen-column format of Lab 2 with the relevance formula and the six quality rules, and explain how it becomes the risk register of Lab 3.

Lesson 1 — Public information sources (1/2) — cyberthreat newsletters and security advisories

Who publishes threat information, what each type of publication contains, and how a small organization keeps watch every week
0:03 – 0:15
Slide 6 · Lesson 1 — Public information sources (1/2)

Objective. Name the six families of public threat-information sources, tell an alert from an advisory and from a newsletter, and build a weekly watch list by matching public items against the Lab 1 asset inventory.

Lesson text — 12 minutes

Slide 7 · Why an analyst reads public sources every week

Why an analyst reads public sources every week

Competency EZ02 says that threat analysis is done based on public information sources: cyberthreat newsletters and frameworks for risk analysis, and that the analyst performs a methodical analysis of public information sources (criterion 2.3). Tonight is that criterion. A public information source is any publication that an organization can read without a contract or a confidential relationship: the alerts of a national cyber security agency, the security advisories of a software vendor, a vulnerability database, a newsletter, an annual report. On Monday you learned who the threat actors are; the public sources tell you what they are doing this week, against which products, and what the publisher recommends.

Three figures from the Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (published May 19, 2026) explain why this reading is not optional. For the first time in nineteen editions, the exploitation of a software vulnerability was the most frequent way into a breached organization (31 % of breaches), ahead of stolen credentials. Ransomware was present in 48 % of breaches. And 48 % of breaches involved a third party. A vulnerability that is exploited at scale is announced publicly, usually within days, by the vendor and by the national agencies. An organization that reads those announcements can act before the attacker reaches it; an organization that does not read them learns about the vulnerability from the attacker.

For Kalmia the point is concrete. The web shop runs WordPress with 23 plugins on top of PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor); four plugins are six months out of date (warning sign W-05), and incident INC-01 was a six-hour outage after a failed plugin update. On October 21, 2026 the PHP project published an emergency release for two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, and the Cyber Centre published alert AL26-026 the same day. Whether Kalmia's hosting provider applied that release is a question the analyst must be able to ask by name, version and date. That is what public sources give you.

Slide 8 · Six families of public sources (1/2)Slide 9 · Six families of public sources (2/2)

Six families of public sources

Public threat information comes from six families of publishers. The family tells you what to expect from the document and how much weight it carries; Lesson 3 will give you a grid to rate each one.

  1. National cyber security authorities. In Canada, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (the Cyber Centre, part of the Communications Security Establishment) publishes alerts and advisories, control-system advisories, guidance documents (the ITSAP [IT Security Awareness Publication series of the Cyber Centre] and ITSM [IT Security Management publication series of the Cyber Centre] series) and strategic assessments such as the National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 and the Ransomware Threat Outlook 2025 to 2027. In the United States, CISA publishes advisories, alerts and the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. Partner agencies (the United Kingdom's NCSC [National Cyber Security Centre, United Kingdom], France's ANSSI [Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information, France], Germany's BSI [Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik, Germany], Australia's ACSC [Australian Cyber Security Centre]) often co-sign the same advisories.
  2. Software and hardware vendors. Every serious vendor publishes security advisories: Microsoft through the Security Update Guide and its monthly release on the second Tuesday (the next one is November 10, 2026), the WordPress project through its security releases, the PHP project through advisories on its repository, the vendors of Kalmia's NAS (network-attached storage), cameras, POS (point of sale) tablets and firewall through their own support pages. The vendor is the primary source for two facts that no one else can confirm: which versions are affected and which version fixes the problem.
  3. Vulnerability and attack-technique databases. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) list, the NVD (National Vulnerability Database), the EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) scores, the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge). They are the subject of Lesson 2.
  4. Computer emergency response teams and information-sharing centres. A CERT (computer emergency response team) or CSIRT (computer security incident response team) is a team that handles incidents for a country, a sector or a company and publishes what it learns; an ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Center) is a sharing centre for one sector. The MS-ISAC advisories of the Center for Internet Security are written for small public organizations and are a good model of a clear advisory. FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), the global association of response teams, maintains the standards used by all of them: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), EPSS and TLP (Traffic Light Protocol).
  5. Newsletters and digests. A cyberthreat newsletter is a periodic summary, usually by e-mail, of the week's threats, vulnerabilities and incidents, with a short comment and links to the original documents. SANS NewsBites (twice a week) and the daily diaries and StormCast of the SANS Internet Storm Center are free examples; the Cyber Centre and CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) both offer e-mail subscriptions to their alerts. A newsletter is a secondary source: it points to the primary document, and the analyst reads the primary document before acting.
  6. Research and industry reports. Annual studies built on incident data: the Verizon DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report), Mandiant M-Trends 2026 (incident-response cases; voice phishing became the second most common initial infection vector), the ENISA Threat Landscape. They do not tell you about this week's vulnerability; they tell you which threat events are frequent, which is exactly what the likelihood column of Lab 3 needs.
Slide 10 · Alert, advisory, bulletin, newsletter — four words that are not synonyms

Alert, advisory, bulletin, newsletter — four words that are not synonyms

The Cyber Centre's own definitions are the ones we use. An alert is used to raise awareness of a recently identified cyber threat that may impact cyber information assets, and to provide additional detection and mitigation advice; it is published when a threat is active or when a vulnerability is critical enough to need immediate attention, and it is updated as the situation changes (AL26-026 reached Update 2 within a week). An advisory announces that a vendor has released a security update for a product and lists the affected and fixed versions; the Cyber Centre publishes several every day, numbered AV26-nnn. A security bulletin is the vendor's own publication of the same facts. A newsletter summarizes several of these for a general audience. Only the first three are primary sources.

Two more terms you will see on every page. An indicator of compromise (IOC [indicator of compromise]) is an observable artefact of an attack — an address, a domain name, a file hash, a sender address — that a defender can search for in logs. The tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs [tactics, techniques and procedures]) of an actor are the behaviours behind the indicators: how it gets in, how it moves, what it takes. Indicators change daily; behaviours change slowly. Lesson 2 shows how behaviours are named with ATT&CK identifiers.

Slide 11 · The weekly watch routine of a small organization

The weekly watch routine of a small organization

A company of 46 people has no analyst on duty, so the routine has to fit in twenty minutes a day and one hour on Friday. It rests on two documents you already have. The first is the asset inventory of Lab 1: the software list with vendor, product and version is the filter that decides whether an item concerns you. The second is a source register: one row per source with its publisher, address, type (alert, advisory, newsletter, report), cadence, how it is received (e-mail, RSS [Really Simple Syndication] feed, web page) and the asset types it covers. Eight to twelve sources are enough for Kalmia: the Cyber Centre alerts and advisories, CISA's KEV additions, Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the WordPress and plugin advisories, the NAS and camera vendors' pages, the POS and loyalty providers' status pages, one newsletter.

The routine itself has four steps. Collect: open the sources on the register, in the same order every day. Filter: keep an item only if its product and version appear in the inventory, or if it describes a threat event that fits Kalmia's exposure facts of Class 4 (for example a vishing campaign against help desks concerns Kalmia because InfoNord runs its help desk). Record: one line per kept item in the watch list — date, source, item, affected Kalmia asset, severity as published, recommended action, owner, deadline. Decide: four outcomes — act now and catalogue (a critical or exploited vulnerability on an exposed asset, or an active campaign: an owner and a date today), add to the threat catalogue (Lesson 4) without urgency, watch (a supplier's product, an announced release, an informational notice: re-check next week or ask the supplier), or discard (no product of the inventory). A discarded item still gets one line — the title, the reason and, in Lesson 3, its rating — so that nobody re-reads it next week; the inventory is the reason, and the inventory is written down.

The rule of this course applies to every source you open

Reading an alert is information gathering. Opening the command-and-control address it lists, downloading a sample it mentions or contacting the people behind a campaign is interaction with malicious infrastructure, prohibited by section 7.3 of the Legal Notice. Check every link on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing before you click (section 14.2 and Annex C); the official sources listed at the end of this module have been checked for you on November 5, 2026.

Key terms to learn

public information source
A publication anyone can read without a contract: agency alerts and advisories, vendor bulletins, vulnerability databases, newsletters, annual reports.
alert
Cyber Centre publication that raises awareness of an active threat or a critical vulnerability and gives detection and mitigation advice (AL26-nnn).
advisory
Notice that a vendor released a security update, with affected and fixed versions (Cyber Centre AV26-nnn; vendor security bulletin).
cyberthreat newsletter
Periodic digest of threats, vulnerabilities and incidents with links to the primary documents — a secondary source.
indicator of compromise (IOC)
Observable artefact of an attack (address, domain, file hash) that can be searched for in logs.
TTP
Tactics, techniques and procedures — the behaviours of an actor, named with ATT&CK identifiers.
source register
One row per source: publisher, address, type, cadence, delivery channel, asset types covered.
watch list
The kept items of the week with the affected asset, the published severity, the recommended action, an owner and a deadline.
primary vs secondary source
The vendor or the agency that observed the fact is primary; a newsletter or a news article that reports it is secondary.

Real-life example 1 — Kalmia's watch list for the week of November 2, 2026

Slide 12 · Real-life example 1 — Kalmia's watch list, week of November 2, 2026
Task

From eight public items published between October 15 and November 5, 2026 — four Cyber Centre alerts, one Microsoft release note, one WordPress plugin advisory, one POS provider status notice and one newsletter item — decide which items concern Kalmia by matching them against the Lab 1 software inventory and the Class 4 exposure facts, and write the watch list: asset, severity, action, owner, deadline, decision.

How it relates to this lecture

This is the four-step routine of Lesson 1 applied to one week: collect from the source register, filter with the inventory, record, decide. The decision column uses the three outcomes of the lesson (act now, add to the catalogue, watch).

Where it goes next (future labs)

Interactive example 1 — The weekly advisory filter (Bash)

Slide 13 · Interactive example 1 — the weekly advisory filter (Bash)
Interactive example — task

A Bash script reads one week of public items exported from the source register (advisories_week45.csv) and Kalmia's software keyword list exported from the Lab 1 inventory (kalmia_keywords.csv), keeps the items whose product keywords match an asset, counts the kept and discarded items per source family, and writes the watch list (advisory_watchlist.csv) with the published severity and the decision.

How it relates to the lecture

It is the filter step of the weekly routine of Lesson 1: the inventory decides what is kept. The script uses only standard shell tools (grep, awk, sort), so it runs on the Git Bash of a Windows laptop as well as on macOS or Linux — the point is the method, not the tool.

The frame below replays the recorded execution of the script — the real run of November 5, 2026 on the data files — one statement at a time: Start / Pause, Step, Next event, Restart, the speed selector, the current line highlighted in the source, every step written in the execution window and the drawing updated by the markers the script prints. Language: Bash. The script has a comment before every line; the listing is under the frame.

Interactive example 1 — The weekly advisory filter (Bash)
The code of the example — a comment before every line (click to show / hide; use Copy code above)
Step by step — what the example does
  1. The script loads the keyword list: one line per Kalmia product with the asset identifier of Lab 1 (for example php,A-16, windows 10,A-09;A-12, updraftplus,A-16).
  2. It reads the week's items line by line (date, source, family, title, products, severity, reference) and lowers the case of the product field so that 'PHP' and 'php' compare equal.
  3. For each item it searches every keyword in the product field; the first match gives the asset identifier, and the item is written to the kept list with that identifier. An item with no match is counted as discarded, with its source family.
  4. A severity rule turns the published severity into a decision: Critical or High on a matched asset → act now; Medium or an active campaign → catalogue; Informational → watch.
  5. The execution window shows one line per item (kept or discarded, why), then the counts per family; the drawing shows the funnel (items in → matched → act now) and the bar per source family filling as the script runs.
  6. Start runs automatically, Pause stops after the current item, Step advances by one item, Restart clears everything; Copy copies the complete commented script; Download saves the script, the two input files and the resulting watch list.

Lesson 2 — Public information sources (2/2) — CVE and MITRE ATT&CK
One identifier per vulnerability, one identifier per attacker behaviour — and the scores that tell you how urgent each one is
0:15 – 0:30
Slide 16 · Lesson 2 — Public information sources (2/2)
Objective. Read a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) record (identifier, CNA [CVE Numbering Authority], affected versions, CVSS [Common Vulnerability Scoring System], CWE [Common Weakness Enumeration], KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] status) and an ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) page (tactic, technique, sub-technique, group, mitigation), and use both identifiers to write a threat event that names a Kalmia asset.
Lesson text — 15 minutes
Slide 17 · A CVE record — one identifier for one vulnerability
CVE — one identifier for one vulnerability


A CVE record is the public description of one vulnerability in one or more products, with a unique identifier of the form CVE-YYYY-NNNNN: the year the identifier was reserved, then a sequence number of four or more digits. The identifier is the only part that never changes; everything else can be updated. The CVE Program has run since 1999, is operated by the MITRE Corporation and sponsored by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), and it does not find vulnerabilities itself: records are created by CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) — vendors, open-source projects, research companies and national agencies authorized to assign identifiers for a defined scope. There were 502 of them on March 31, 2026. The PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) project is a CNA; so are Microsoft, Google, Wordfence and Patchstack (the two largest publishers of WordPress plugin vulnerabilities), VulDB and the Linux kernel.


The volume is the first thing a beginner must understand. 48,185 records were published in 2025, about 15,000 per quarter in 2026, more than 340,000 since the start of the program. Nobody reads them all; the inventory filter of Lesson 1 and the three scores below exist precisely because of that volume.


Open the record of CVE-2026-109618 and you find the fields that every record carries since the JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) 5 format. The metadata: identifier, the CNA that published it (php), the state (Published; the other states are Reserved, before publication, and Rejected, when an identifier turns out to be a duplicate or not a vulnerability), the dates of publication and of the last update (October 21 and November 5, 2026). The CNA container: a title (RCE [remote code execution] via OOM [out of memory] corruption), a description, the affected products with their version ranges and the version that fixes each branch (8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12), the problem type as a CWE identifier (CWE-416, use after free), the metrics (CVSS v4.0 base score 9.2, Critical) and the references (the vendor advisory, mailing lists, the KEV catalogue — CISA added both PHP vulnerabilities to it on October 26, 2026, with a federal deadline of October 29). Since 2024 a second container may follow, the ADP (Authorized Data Publisher) container of CISA, which adds a decision-tree rating (SSVC [Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization]) and, when it applies, the date the vulnerability entered the KEV catalogue.


The NVD (National Vulnerability Database), run by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), republishes every record and used to add its own analysis to all of them — product names in a normalized form (CPE [Common Platform Enumeration]), a CVSS score when the CNA gave none, the weakness type. That changed on April 15, 2026: faced with a record volume it could no longer process, NIST moved to a risk-based model. It now enriches first the CVEs in the KEV catalogue and those affecting critical software; the rest are listed with the status Not Scheduled and carry only what the CNA wrote, and the unenriched backlog published before March 1, 2026 was moved to that status. The practical consequence for you: the score in the CNA's own record is often the only score, which is why Lesson 3 asks who published a number before trusting it.


Slide 18 · Three scores that answer three different questionsSlide 19 · CVSS bands and the four questions of BOD 26-04
Three scores that answer three different questions


  • CVSS — how severe is it? The Common Vulnerability Scoring System of FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) gives a base score from 0.0 to 10.0 computed from a vector string that lists the metrics: in version 4.0, the attack vector (network, adjacent, local, physical), attack complexity, attack requirements, privileges required, user interaction, and the impact on the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the vulnerable system and of subsequent systems. The qualitative bands are None (0.0), Low (0.1–3.9), Medium (4.0–6.9), High (7.0–8.9) and Critical (9.0–10.0). Version 3.1 is still common in older records. CVSS measures the technical severity of the flaw; it says nothing about whether anyone exploits it or whether you run the product.
  • EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) — how likely is exploitation soon? The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, also from FIRST, publishes every day for every CVE a probability between 0 and 1 that it will be exploited in the next 30 days, computed from observed exploitation data; a percentile shows where the CVE ranks among all others.
  • KEV — is it exploited now? The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue of CISA lists the CVEs for which there is reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild and a clear remediation. About 1,700 entries in 2026, against more than 340,000 CVEs: the KEV list is small and every entry is urgent. CISA created it in November 2021 with Binding Operational Directive 22-01; on June 10, 2026 BOD 26-04 replaced the fixed deadlines with a four-variable model — is the asset publicly exposed, is the CVE in the KEV, is exploitation automatable, does it give full control — and five remediation tiers, the shortest being three days. The directive binds US federal agencies, but its logic is exactly the one a small organization should copy: an exposed asset with a KEV entry is fixed first, whatever its CVSS score.


Keep the three apart: CVSS is severity, EPSS is probability, KEV is evidence. In Lab 3 the likelihood column will use EPSS and KEV; the impact column will use the CVSS impact metrics together with the business impact analysis of Lab 1.


Slide 20 · MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise v20 — fifteen tactics (October 13, 2026)Slide 21 · ATT&CK — tactic, technique, sub-technique, procedure
MITRE ATT&CK — one identifier for one attacker behaviour


MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) is a knowledge base of the behaviours that attackers have actually been observed using, maintained by the MITRE Corporation and free to use. It is organized in three matrices — Enterprise (servers, workstations, cloud, identity), Mobile and ICS (industrial control systems) — and it is updated twice a year. The current version is v20, published on October 13, 2026; the Enterprise matrix contains 15 tactics, 227 techniques, 479 sub-techniques, 178 groups, 842 pieces of software and 57 campaigns, plus 44 mitigations and the detection strategies and analytics added since 2025.


Four words carry the structure. A tactic is the attacker's goal at one stage of an intrusion — the why: get in, run code, stay, escalate, hide, steal credentials, look around, move, collect, control, take out, do damage. A technique is one way of reaching that goal — the how: Phishing (T1566) is a technique of the Initial Access tactic. A sub-technique is a more specific way: Spearphishing Voice (T1566.004) is the help-desk telephone call of AL26-028. A procedure is what a specific group or malware actually did with the technique, with its source report. Identifiers follow the object type: TA for tactics, T for techniques, G for groups (G0046 FIN7), S for software (S0154 Cobalt Strike), C for campaigns, M for mitigations (M1032 Multi-factor Authentication).


The fifteen Enterprise tactics of v20, in the order of the matrix: Reconnaissance (TA0043), Resource Development (TA0042), Initial Access (TA0001), Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Privilege Escalation (TA0004), Stealth (TA0005), Defense Impairment (TA0112), Credential Access (TA0006), Discovery (TA0007), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Command and Control (TA0011), Exfiltration (TA0010), Impact (TA0040). Two of them are new names: v20 split the former Defense Evasion tactic into Stealth (blending in with normal activity) and Defense Impairment (breaking security tools so that defenders lose visibility). If you read a report written before October 2026, 'defense evasion' maps onto one of these two.


Slide 22 · Why the two identifiers belong in the catalogue
Why the two identifiers belong in a threat catalogue


A threat event written in plain words — an attacker takes over the web shop — cannot be compared with another organization's rows, cannot be linked to a mitigation, and cannot be verified. The same event written with identifiers — a cybercriminal exploits CVE-2026-109618 on the web shop (A-16) through T1190, Exploit Public-Facing Application — can be. The CVE identifier ties the event to a vendor advisory with a fixed version (the evidence); the technique identifier ties it to ATT&CK's mitigations and detections, which Lab 4 will use, and to the groups known to use it, which supports the capability rating of Class 4. For Kalmia's documented facts the mapping is short: INC-02 is T1657 Financial Theft reached through phishing; INC-04 is T1078 Valid Accounts (the former supervisor's account); INC-05 is T1566.002 Spearphishing Link by text message; the always-connected backup disk is what makes T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact catastrophic; RoastLink on ROAST-PC is T1133 External Remote Services. The free ATT&CK Navigator colours the techniques you select on the matrix and exports the picture — that is how Lab 2 will show Kalmia's techniques on one page.


A CVE is a vulnerability, not a threat
The catalogue of Lesson 4 lists threat events, and a threat event needs a source who acts. The CVE record is the evidence that a technique is possible on a given product version; the threat source (Class 4) is who would use it; the asset (Lab 1) is where. Topic 4 (Classes 6 and 9) studies the vulnerabilities themselves; tonight you only borrow the CVE identifier as evidence.
Key terms to learn
CVE record
Public description of one vulnerability with a unique identifier CVE-YYYY-NNNNN, affected and fixed versions, weakness type, metrics and references.
CVE Numbering Authority (CNA)
Organization authorized to assign identifiers and publish records for a defined scope (502 in March 2026).
CVSS
0.0–10.0 severity score computed from a vector string; bands None, Low, Medium, High, Critical; v4.0 current, v3.1 still common.
EPSS
Daily probability (0–1) that a CVE is exploited in the next 30 days.
KEV catalogue
CISA's list of CVEs with reliable evidence of exploitation; about 1,700 entries in 2026; a KEV entry is fixed first.
CWE
Common Weakness Enumeration — the class of programming or design weakness behind a CVE (CWE-416 use after free).
NVD
NIST's enriched copy of the CVE list; since April 15, 2026, enrichment by risk priority, other records 'Not Scheduled'.
ATT&CK tactic / technique / sub-technique / procedure
Goal (why) / method (how) / specific method / observed implementation by a named group.
ATT&CK v20
October 13, 2026: Enterprise 15 tactics, 227 techniques, 479 sub-techniques; Defense Evasion split into Stealth and Defense Impairment.

Five records, five different outcomes, and none of them depends on the CVSS number alone. The first row is the one Nadia Roy hears about tonight: a Critical, exploited, network-reachable vulnerability on the system that brings a quarter of the revenue, two months before the holiday season. The last row shows the other half of the method: a KEV entry with a High score that does not concern Kalmia at all, discarded in one line because the inventory says so. A PowerShell script reads a file of CVE records (cve_records.json, five real records trimmed to the fields of the CVE JSON 5.1 format: metadata, affected products and versions, CVSS metrics, CWE, KEV date) and Kalmia's software list (kalmia_software.csv, from the Lab 1 inventory with an 'exposed to the Internet' flag), matches each record's product against the list, attaches the ATT&CK technique from a small mapping table, applies the four questions of BOD 26-04 to set a deadline, and writes cve_exposure.csv.
How it relates to the lecture

The frame below replays the recorded execution of the script — the real run of November 5, 2026 on the data files — one statement at a time: Start / Pause, Step, Next event, Restart, the speed selector, the current line highlighted in the source, every step written in the execution window and the drawing updated by the markers the script prints. Interactive example 2 — CVE records to exposure table (PowerShell)
The code of the example — a comment before every line (click to show / hide; use Copy code above)
Step by step — what the example does
  1. The script loads kalmia_software.csv (asset identifier, vendor, product, version, exposed yes/no) and cve_records.json (an array of records in the structure of the CVE JSON 5.1 format).
  2. For each record it reads the metadata (identifier, CNA, publication date), the first affected product with its version range and fixed version, the CVSS score and version, the first CWE, and the KEV date in the CISA ADP container if there is one.
  3. It compares the product name of the record with every product of the inventory (case-insensitive 'contains' on normalized names) and keeps the first match with its asset identifier and exposure flag; no match means 'discard' with the reason.
  4. A mapping table turns the CWE and the product type into the ATT&CK technique an attacker would use (web application weakness → T1190; remote support product → T1133; library in a browser → T1203; local privilege flaw → T1068).
  5. The four questions of BOD 26-04 are answered from the data — exposed (inventory flag), KEV (date present), automatable (attack vector network and no user interaction in the vector string), full control (impact metrics High on confidentiality, integrity and availability) — and the combination gives the tier, in the simplified reading of Table 1 (Appendix A of the directive) used in this course: KEV entry with full control, or exposed with automatable exploitation and full control → 3 days (with a check for an existing compromise when the CVE is in the KEV); any other combination with a KEV entry, or exposed with automatable exploitation or full control → 14 days; any other combination with at least one 'yes' → 60 days; no 'yes' at all → the next scheduled upgrade. The directive itself maps all sixteen combinations; its five tiers run from three days to the next upgrade.
  6. The execution window prints one block per record; the drawing shows the fifteen ATT&CK tactics as columns with the matched technique lit in its tactic, a CVSS gauge per record and a KEV badge. Start, Pause, Step, Restart, Copy and the downloads work as in example 1.

Lesson 3 — Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report
Seven questions in a fixed order, two six-level scales, the estimative words of the Cyber Centre and the TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) markings
0:30 – 0:45
Slide 27 · Lesson 3 — Methodical analysis of public sources
Objective. Read any alert, advisory or report with the seven questions, separate facts from assessments, rate the source (A–F) and the information (1–6), rate its relevance to the organization, respect its TLP marking, and record a decision with its reasons.
Lesson text — 15 minutes
Slide 28 · Why a method, and not a reading
Why a method, and not a reading


A threat report is any document that describes a threat, a vulnerability, a campaign or an incident: an alert, an advisory, a vendor bulletin, a research blog post, an annual assessment. Two analysts who read the same report without a method reach different conclusions, and neither can explain why. The competency asks for a methodical analysis: the same questions, in the same order, with the answers written down, so that a colleague — or the professor marking Lab 2 — can check them. The method below has seven questions. The first three are about the document, the next two about the organization, the last two about the decision. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-150, the guide to cyber threat information sharing, describes the same discipline for organizations that consume shared information: know the source, evaluate the quality, decide how it may be used.


Slide 29 · The seven questions (1/2) — about the documentSlide 30 · The seven questions (2/2) — about us, and the decision
The seven questions


  1. Who publishes it, when, and under which marking? Identify the publisher and its family (Lesson 1), the date, the version or update number, and the TLP marking. A report with no date or no identifiable publisher fails this question and is rated F6 below.
  2. What is it about? A vulnerability (which products, which versions), a campaign (which technique, which victims), an actor (which motivation, which capability), or an incident. Write the subject in one sentence of your own.
  3. What is the evidence? Separate what the publisher observed (a patch was released; exploitation was seen; infrastructure was identified) from what it assesses (an actor is probably responsible; exploitation is likely to follow). The words used are the signal: the Cyber Centre's assessments use estimative language with defined ranges — almost no chance (1–9 %), very unlikely (10–24 %), unlikely (25–39 %), roughly even chance (40–59 %), likely (60–74 %), very likely (75–89 %), almost certainly (90–99 %) — and may add a confidence level (low, moderate, high) that describes the quality of the sources and reasoning behind the judgment, the practice set out in ODNI Intelligence Community Directive 203. Attribution to a named group or state is always an assessment: you report who made it, you never repeat it as a fact (Legal Notice, section 7.3). Then rate the source and the information with the two scales below.
  4. Does it apply to us? Match the products and versions against the Lab 1 inventory and the described threat event against the exposure facts of Class 4. Write the asset identifiers. Relevance is High when an exposed asset or an exposure fact is matched directly, Moderate when the match is indirect or depends on a supplier, Low or none otherwise.
  5. How does the threat act? Translate the behaviour into ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) identifiers (Lesson 2) and list the indicators of compromise the report gives. Indicators are copied into the record for the people who run the logs; they are never tested by visiting them.
  6. What does the publisher recommend, and can we do it? Fixed versions, configuration changes, awareness messages, detection advice. Name the owner at the organization who can act, and the supplier when the asset is hosted or managed by someone else.
  7. What is our decision, and where is it recorded? Act now, add to the threat catalogue, watch, or discard — with the ratings and the reasons on the same line of the watch list. A decision without its reasons cannot be reviewed.


Slide 31 · Two scales for one report — source reliability × information credibilitySlide 32 · Estimative language and confidence — reading an assessment
Two scales for one report: source reliability and information credibility


Intelligence services have rated information for eighty years with the same two scales, now codified in the NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) standard AJP-2.1 and reproduced in the United States Army manual FM 2-22.3, Appendix B, and known as the Admiralty or NATO system. The source reliability scale rates the publisher's record, from A (completely reliable) to E (unreliable), with F when it cannot be judged. The information credibility scale rates the statement itself, from 1 (confirmed by other independent sources) to 5 (improbable), with 6 when it cannot be judged. The two are rated independently and written together: a Cyber Centre alert that repeats a vendor advisory with the fixed versions is A1; a recognized researcher's blog post that reports a proof of concept nobody else has confirmed is B2 or B3; an anonymous social-media post with no product, no version and no reference is F6. The point of two scales is that a usually reliable source can publish an unconfirmed item (B3), and an unknown source can publish something that other sources confirm (F1); the analyst keeps the two judgments apart. The open-source platform OpenCTI stores exactly these two values on every report; the catalogue of Lab 2 stores them in two columns.


Source reliabilityMeaningInformation credibilityMeaning
A — Completely reliableA primary source with a long record of accuracy (the vendor of the product; a national agency).1 — Confirmed by other sourcesIndependent sources say the same thing; consistent with what is already known.
B — Usually reliableA recognized research company or response team; minor past errors.2 — Probably trueNot confirmed, but logical and consistent with other information.
C — Fairly reliableA known publication whose record is mixed or short.3 — Possibly trueReasonably logical; agrees with some other information.
D — Not usually reliableA source with a record of errors or of commercial exaggeration.4 — DoubtfulNot logical, or contradicted by other information.
E — UnreliableA source that has published false information before.5 — ImprobableIllogical and contradicted by other information.
F — Cannot be judgedNo record: an anonymous account, a new site, a forwarded message.6 — Cannot be judgedNo basis to evaluate the information.


Slide 33 · TLP 2.0 — what you may do with a report
TLP 2.0 — what you may do with a report


The Traffic Light Protocol of FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), version 2.0 since August 2022, is a set of five markings that the publisher puts on a report to say who may receive it: TLP:CLEAR — No limit on disclosure — public information. Agency alerts and CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) records are TLP:CLEAR.; TLP:GREEN — May be shared within the community (sector, peers), not published on the Internet.; TLP:AMBER — May be shared within the organization and with its clients on a need-to-know basis.; TLP:AMBER+STRICT — May be shared within the organization only.; TLP:RED — For the named recipients only — not even within their organization.. Everything you read in this course is TLP:CLEAR. The marking matters in two directions: you respect it when you receive a report from a supplier or a sharing group, and you apply the same idea to your own work — the Lab 2 catalogue shows exactly what an attacker would want to know about Kalmia, which is why section 7.5 of the Legal Notice keeps it confidential to the course.


Slide 34 · Six errors the method prevents
Six errors the method prevents


  • Reading severity as risk: a Critical score on a product you do not run is not a risk for you (question 4 before question 3).
  • Copying a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score into the likelihood column: CVSS is severity; likelihood comes from KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities), EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), exposure and the actor's intent.
  • Acting on a secondary source: the newsletter says 'critical', the vendor bulletin says 'fixed in 1.26.5' — only the second one tells you what to do.
  • Repeating an attribution as a fact: 'the Cyber Centre assesses that…' is correct; 'group X attacked…' is not, unless the group claimed it and the report says so.
  • Ignoring the date and the update number: AL26-026 changed twice in six days; a decision taken on the first version must be re-read on the third.
  • Testing an indicator by visiting it: an address in a report is copied for the log search; opening it is interaction with malicious infrastructure (section 7.3).
Key terms to learn
threat report
Any document describing a threat, vulnerability, campaign or incident: alert, advisory, bulletin, blog post, annual assessment.
the seven questions
Publisher/date/marking · subject · evidence (facts vs assessments, ratings) · applicability (assets, relevance) · behaviour (ATT&CK, indicators) · recommendations/owner · decision and record.
source reliability (A–F)
Rating of the publisher's record: A completely reliable … E unreliable, F cannot be judged (NATO AJP-2.1 / Admiralty system).
information credibility (1–6)
Rating of the statement: 1 confirmed by other sources … 5 improbable, 6 cannot be judged; rated independently of the source.
estimative language
Defined probability words: almost no chance 1–9 % … almost certainly 90–99 % (Cyber Centre scale).
confidence level
Low, moderate or high — the quality of the sources and reasoning behind an assessment, not its probability.
attribution
The assessment that a named actor is responsible; reported with its author ('CISA [Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency] assesses…'), never repeated as a fact.
TLP 2.0
CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT, RED — who may receive a report; public alerts are TLP:CLEAR.
relevance
High: an exposed asset or an exposure fact matched directly; Moderate: indirect or through a supplier; Low/none: no match.

Two documents, four catalogue rows, two 'act now' decisions with owners and dates; one document discarded in one line with its rating. Every judgment is written where the next reader can check it: the source rating next to the source, the relevance next to the asset identifiers, the ATT&CK identifiers next to the behaviour. Step by step — what the example does
  1. The page holds the three documents as data: for each one, the text (summarized), the answers to the seven questions and, for each answer, the start and end of the passage to highlight.

Questions 2 to 7 follow in order; at question 3 the source letter and the information digit are set and the marker appears on the 6 × 6 grid; at question 4 the matched asset identifiers and the relevance badge appear; at question 5 the ATT&CK identifiers are listed; at question 7 the decision badge is set.

List the seven questions of the reading method in order.click to flip
1 publisher, date, marking · 2 subject · 3 evidence, with the source and information ratings · 4 applicability to our assets (relevance) · 5 behaviour (ATT&CK) and indicators · 6 recommendations and owner · 7 decision and record.click to flip back
What is the difference between source reliability and information credibility?click to flip
Reliability (A–F) rates the publisher's record; credibility (1–6) rates the statement itself, by corroboration and logic. They are rated independently: a usually reliable source can publish an unconfirmed item (B3).click to flip back
How do you treat an attribution to a named group in a report?click to flip
As an assessment: you record who made it and with which estimative words or confidence level ('the Cyber Centre assesses…'); you never repeat it as a fact (Legal Notice, section 7.3).click to flip back
What does 'very likely' mean in a Cyber Centre assessment?click to flip
An approximate probability of 75 to 89 %, on the Cyber Centre's estimative language scale (almost no chance 1–9 % … almost certainly 90–99 %); the percentages are judgments, not statistics.click to flip back
What may you do with a TLP:AMBER report received from a supplier?click to flip
Share it inside Kalmia and with Kalmia's clients on a need-to-know basis — not publish it, not post it in a community. TLP:AMBER+STRICT would restrict it to Kalmia only.click to flip back

Lesson 4 — Building a threat catalogue for an organization
From sources, events and assets to the fifteen columns of Kalmia's catalogue — the method, the quality rules and the hand-over to the risk register
0:45 – 0:57
Slide 39 · Lesson 4 — Building a threat catalogue for an organization
Objective. Write threat events in the standard form, assemble them into the catalogue with the fifteen columns of Lab 2, rate relevance with the course formula, check the catalogue against the six quality rules, and explain how it feeds the risk register of Lab 3.
Lesson text — 12 minutes
Slide 40 · What a threat catalogue is — and is not
What a threat catalogue is


A threat catalogue — some organizations say threat register or threat list — is the structured list of the threat sources and threat events that are relevant to an organization's assets, each with the evidence that makes it relevant and the public reference that documents it. It is the deliverable of Lab 2 and the second chapter of the Integrative Project. It is not the risk register: it does not yet say how likely an event is or how much it would cost. Those two numbers are added in Topic 5 and Lab 3, once Topic 4 has supplied the vulnerabilities. The catalogue answers one question only, for every asset of Lab 1: who or what could harm it, how, and what makes us think so?


The method comes from NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1. Its Task 2-1 identifies the threat sources and characterizes the adversarial ones by capability, intent and targeting (Appendix D, the scales you used on Monday); its Task 2-2 identifies the threat events that each source could initiate and gives, in Appendix E, a representative list of adversarial events (reconnaissance, crafting phishing attacks, delivering malware, exploiting vulnerabilities in exposed services, exfiltrating data, conducting denial of service…) and of non-adversarial events (mishandling of information, incorrect privilege settings, failure of a supplier's service, disk errors, fire, flood, power failure). ISO/IEC 27005:2022, the international standard, gives in its Annex A a comparable list of typical threats grouped by origin — physical, natural, infrastructure and technical failures, human actions, compromise of services, organizational. The two lists are checklists: you walk through them asset by asset so that nothing is forgotten, and you keep only what the evidence supports.


Slide 41 · How to write a threat event — one row, one sentence, four parts
How to write a threat event


One row, one event, one sentence with four parts: the source (an actor profile of Class 4 or a non-adversarial source), the action (a verb that corresponds to an ATT&CK [Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge] technique when the source is adversarial), the asset (a Lab 1 identifier) and the means or precondition (the technique's entry point, the exposure fact it relies on). A cybercriminal group encrypts NAS-01 (A-03) and its always-connected backup disk (A-04) after entering with a phished Microsoft 365 password — T1486 is a threat event. Ransomware is not: it is a tool. The NAS (network-attached storage) administrator password is shared by four people is not either: it is a vulnerability, which belongs to Topic 4; the event that uses it is a negligent user's leaked shared password gives an attacker administrator access to NAS-01 — T1078. Keep every event to one technique; if two techniques are needed, write two rows.


Slide 42 · The six stepsSlide 43 · The fifteen columns of Lab 2 (1/2)Slide 44 · The fifteen columns of Lab 2 (2/2) — ratings and evidence
The six steps


  1. Start from the assets and the exposure facts. Open the Lab 1 inventory and the twelve exposure facts of Class 4 (F01 personal information … F12 backup reachable from the network). Every critical asset must end up in at least one row.
  2. List the sources. The four external actor profiles of Class 4 (cybercriminals, hacktivists, state-sponsored groups, opportunistic attackers), the three internal types (malicious insider, negligent or accidental user, third party or supplier) and the three non-adversarial families (accidental, structural, environmental): ten categories. Kalmia's list has twelve named sources (TS-01 to TS-12) because the cybercriminal profile splits into three — ransomware affiliate, opportunistic exploitation, fraud by e-mail — according to the facts of Class 4.
  3. Derive the events. For each source, ask which techniques it uses (ATT&CK, Lesson 2) and against which assets they make sense (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] Appendix E and ISO/IEC [International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission] 27005 Annex A as checklists). Bring in the week's public items (Lessons 1 and 3): an alert or a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) that matches an asset is the evidence of an event, with its source rating.
  4. Merge and split. Two rows with the same source, technique, asset and entry point are one row with two pieces of evidence (the two PHP [PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor] vulnerabilities of October 21 are one event). One row with two techniques, or one technique through two different entry points (the PHP engine and an outdated plugin), is two rows.
  5. Rate. Capability, intent and targeting on the 1–5 scale for adversarial sources (1 · 1 · 1 for the others), the number of exposure facts the event relies on, and the relevance by the course formula — High if intent is at least 4 and capability at least 3, or if three or more facts are matched; Moderate if intent is at least 3 or two facts are matched; Low otherwise. Relevance ranks the rows for Lab 3; it is not a likelihood.
  6. Check the quality. The six rules below, applied before the file is handed in.


Slide 45 · Six quality rules
Six quality rules


  • Complete: every exposure fact (F01–F12), every incident (INC-01 to INC-05) and every critical asset of the business impact analysis appears in at least one row.
  • Specific: every row names a source, a technique or a non-adversarial mechanism, and an asset identifier. 'Hackers attack the company' fails.
  • Evidenced: every row has evidence from Kalmia's documents and a public reference with its date and rating. A row without either is deleted or marked 'to verify'.
  • Threats, not vulnerabilities: a weakness (shared PIN [personal identification number], missing MFA [multi-factor authentication], flat network) is written in the evidence column of the event that uses it, never as a row of its own.
  • Factual and ethical: no person is named as a culprit; findings describe accounts and processes (INC-04 is 'a former employee's account was not disabled', not a name). Attribution is reported as the publisher's assessment. All data is fictional (Legal Notice, sections 6.7, 7.3, 7.5 and 18).
  • Consistent: identifiers match the Lab 1 inventory, the source names match the Class 4 profiles, the technique identifiers exist in ATT&CK v20, and the file keeps the fifteen columns in order so that the checker script and the marker can read it.


Slide 46 · From the catalogue to the risk register — Labs 3 and 4
From the catalogue to the risk register


Lab 3 will take each catalogue row, attach the vulnerabilities that Topic 4 finds on the asset, and rate two things that the catalogue deliberately leaves out: the likelihood that the event occurs (from the source's intent and targeting, the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] and EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System] data, the incident history, the exposure facts) and the impact if it does (from the business impact analysis of Lab 1 and the CVSS [Common Vulnerability Scoring System] impact metrics). Likelihood times impact gives the risk score, and the risk register is the catalogue sorted by that score. Lab 4 then answers the top of the register with controls — and the ATT&CK identifiers you write tonight are what will let you pull the matching mitigations in one step. This is why the catalogue is built with identifiers and evidence rather than with adjectives: everything that follows is computed from it.


Confidentiality of the catalogue
A finished catalogue tells an attacker which assets matter, which accounts are weak and which suppliers have access. Section 7.5 of the Legal Notice and section 18.2 apply: the file stays in the course folder, is shared only with the professor through Léa, contains fictional data only, and is never presented as an audit of a real organization.
Key terms to learn
threat catalogue
Structured list of threat sources and threat events relevant to an organization's assets, each with evidence and a public reference; the deliverable of Lab 2.
threat source
Who or what can initiate a threat event: adversarial (actor profiles), accidental, structural, environmental (NIST SP [Special Publication] 800-30 Appendix D).
threat event
One sentence: source + action (technique) + asset + means or precondition; one technique per row.
NIST SP 800-30 Tasks 2-1 and 2-2
Identify threat sources (with capability, intent, targeting) and identify threat events (Appendix E checklists).
ISO/IEC 27005:2022 Annex A
Examples of typical threats by origin: physical, natural, failures, human actions, compromise of services, organizational.
relevance formula
High if (Intent ≥ 4 and Capability ≥ 3) or facts ≥ 3; Moderate if Intent ≥ 3 or facts ≥ 2; otherwise Low — a ranking, not a likelihood.
six quality rules
Complete · specific · evidenced · threats not vulnerabilities · factual and ethical · consistent.
risk register
The catalogue extended with vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact and sorted by risk score — Lab 3.

Run the six rules on the fifteen rows. Complete: eleven of the twelve exposure facts, all five incidents and every critical asset of Lab 1 appear (F11, information of state interest, is absent because Kalmia holds none — the absence is written in the Lab 2 notes). Specific: every row has a source, a mechanism and an asset identifier. Evidenced: every row has Kalmia evidence and a rated reference. Threats, not vulnerabilities: W-03, W-04, W-05 and W-07 appear only in the evidence column. Factual: no person is named. Consistent: the identifiers come from Lab 1 and Class 4, and every technique exists in ATT&CK v20. Six rows are High, seven Moderate, two Low — the order in which Lab 3 will rate them. Interactive example 4 builds these rows from three input files and runs the same checks, which is exactly what the Lab 2 checker will do on your file.
Interactive example 4 — Catalogue builder and Lab 2 checker (Python)
Slide 48 · Interactive example 4 — building the catalogue (Python 3)
Interactive example — task
A Python script reads three files — threat_sources.csv (the twelve sources with family, side and capability, intent, targeting), threat_events.csv (the events with their technique, asset identifiers, exposure facts, evidence, reference and source rating) and assets.csv (the Lab 1 identifiers) — joins them, computes the relevance of each row with the course formula, merges duplicates, applies the six quality rules and writes threat_catalogue.csv with a summary. The same script, run with --check on a student's catalogue, reports the rows that break a rule: the Lab 2 readiness checker.
How it relates to the lecture
It automates steps 3 to 6 of Lesson 4 and makes the quality rules executable: a row without an asset identifier, without evidence or without a public reference is reported, a duplicate is merged, and the relevance column is computed rather than typed. The checker mode is given to the students so that they can test their Lab 2 file before submitting it.
The frame below replays the recorded execution of the script — the real run of November 5, 2026 on the data files — one statement at a time: Start / Pause, Step, Next event, Restart, the speed selector, the current line highlighted in the source, every step written in the execution window and the drawing updated by the markers the script prints. Language: Python. The script has a comment before every line; the listing is under the frame.
Interactive example 4 — Catalogue builder and Lab 2 checker (Python)
The code of the example — a comment before every line (click to show / hide; use Copy code above)
Step by step — what the example does
  1. The script loads the three CSV (comma-separated values) files with Python's csv module and indexes the sources and assets by identifier.
  2. For each event it looks up the source (family, side, capability, intent, targeting) and checks that every asset identifier exists in the Lab 1 list; an unknown identifier is reported as a rule-6 error.
  3. It computes relevance with the course formula: High if (intent ≥ 4 and capability ≥ 3) or facts ≥ 3; Moderate if intent ≥ 3 or facts ≥ 2; otherwise Low — non-adversarial rows carry 1 · 1 · 1 and depend on the facts only.
  4. It merges rows that share the same source, technique, asset and entry point (step 4), concatenating their evidence, and it flags rows whose event text names a weakness without an action (rule 4) or an event without a technique for an adversarial source (rule 2).
  5. It checks completeness (rule 1): every exposure fact F01–F12, every incident INC-01 to INC-05 and every asset tagged critical in assets.csv must appear in at least one row; missing items are listed.
  6. It writes threat_catalogue.csv (the fifteen columns in the Lab 2 order) and prints the counts per relevance level and per source family; the drawing shows sources, events and assets as three columns with a link drawn for each row as it is built, coloured by relevance, and a checklist of the six rules that turns green or red. In --check mode the same engine runs on the student's file and prints the report without rebuilding anything.

What are the four parts of a threat event sentence?click to flip
Source + action (an ATT&CK technique for adversarial sources) + asset (Lab 1 identifier) + means or precondition. One technique per row.click to flip back
Is 'the NAS administrator password is shared by four people' a catalogue row?click to flip
No — it is a vulnerability (Topic 4) and goes in the evidence column of the event that uses it: 'a leaked shared password gives an attacker administrator access to NAS-01 — T1078'.click to flip back
State the relevance formula of the course.click to flip
High if (intent ≥ 4 and capability ≥ 3) or exposure facts ≥ 3; Moderate if intent ≥ 3 or facts ≥ 2; otherwise Low. Non-adversarial rows carry 1 · 1 · 1, so their relevance depends on the facts only. It ranks rows; it is not a likelihood.click to flip back
Name the six quality rules.click to flip
Complete · specific · evidenced · threats not vulnerabilities · factual and ethical · consistent.click to flip back
What does Lab 3 add to a catalogue row to make it a risk register row?click to flip
The vulnerabilities found in Topic 4, a likelihood rating and an impact rating; likelihood × impact gives the risk score, and the register is the catalogue sorted by that score.click to flip back

Source reliability and information credibility scales (Lesson 3)
Source reliabilityMeaningInformation credibilityMeaning
A — Completely reliableA primary source with a long record of accuracy (the vendor of the product; a national agency).1 — Confirmed by other sourcesIndependent sources say the same thing; consistent with what is already known.
B — Usually reliableA recognized research company or response team; minor past errors.2 — Probably trueNot confirmed, but logical and consistent with other information.
C — Fairly reliableA known publication whose record is mixed or short.3 — Possibly trueReasonably logical; agrees with some other information.
D — Not usually reliableA source with a record of errors or of commercial exaggeration.4 — DoubtfulNot logical, or contradicted by other information.
E — UnreliableA source that has published false information before.5 — ImprobableIllogical and contradicted by other information.
F — Cannot be judgedNo record: an anonymous account, a new site, a forwarded message.6 — Cannot be judgedNo basis to evaluate the information.
TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) 2.0 markings (Lesson 3)
MarkingWho may receive it
TLP:CLEARNo limit on disclosure — public information. Agency alerts and CVE records are TLP:CLEAR.
TLP:GREENMay be shared within the community (sector, peers), not published on the Internet.
TLP:AMBERMay be shared within the organization and with its clients on a need-to-know basis.
TLP:AMBER+STRICTMay be shared within the organization only.
TLP:REDFor the named recipients only — not even within their organization.

Estimative word (Cyber Centre)Approximate probability

Unlikely / improbable25–39 %

Likely / probably60–74 %
Very likely / very probable75–89 %

The seven questions for reading a threat report (Lesson 3)
#QuestionWhat it produces
1Who publishes it, when, under which marking?Publisher family, date, update number, TLP
2What is it about?One-sentence subject: products and versions, or campaign, actor, incident

4Does it apply to us?Asset identifiers matched; relevance High / Moderate / Low
5How does the threat act?ATT&CK identifiers; indicators copied (never visited)

The six quality rules of a threat catalogue (Lesson 4)
RuleTestTypical failure
CompleteEvery exposure fact, incident and critical asset appears in a row (or its absence is explained)No row for INC-03 because 'it was not an attack'
SpecificSource + action + asset identifier in every row'Hackers attack the company'
EvidencedKalmia evidence and a dated, rated public reference in every rowA row copied from a vendor's marketing page without evidence
Threats, not vulnerabilitiesWeaknesses appear only in the evidence column'Shared manager PIN (personal identification number)' as a row
Factual and ethicalNo person named as guilty; attribution reported as an assessment; fictional data'Émilie stole the list'
ConsistentIdentifiers from Lab 1 and Class 4; techniques exist in ATT&CK v20; fifteen columns in orderA-99 that is not in the inventory; T9999

  • CVE Program (cve.org) — The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures program: one identifier per publicly disclosed vulnerability. Operated by MITRE, sponsored by CISA; 502 CVE Numbering Authorities in March 2026; 48,185 records published in 2025 and about 15,000 per quarter in 2026. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • CVE-2026-109618 — the CVE record (cve.org) — The record used in Lesson 2: PHP remote code execution, published October 21, 2026 by the PHP CNA (CVE Numbering Authority), CVSS v4.0 base score 9.2 (Critical), CWE-416, fixed in PHP 8.2.35 / 8.3.36 / 8.4.27 / 8.5.12. (lesson 2,3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)'s enriched copy of the CVE list (CVSS, CPE [Common Platform Enumeration] product names, CWE [Common Weakness Enumeration]). Since April 15, 2026 the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) enriches CVEs by risk priority (KEV entries and critical software first); other records are listed as 'Not Scheduled' and carry only the CNA's data. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST — NVD operations update to address record CVE growth (April 15, 2026) — The announcement of the risk-based enrichment model and of the 'Not Scheduled' status for the pre-March 2026 backlog. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • FIRST — Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 — The specification of the 0–10 severity score and its vector string; v4.0 (November 2023) is current, v3.1 is still widely used. Qualitative bands: None 0.0, Low 0.1–3.9, Medium 4.0–6.9, High 7.0–8.9, Critical 9.0–10.0. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • FIRST — Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) — A daily probability (0 to 1) that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, computed from observed exploitation data. Complements CVSS (severity) and KEV (confirmed exploitation). (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • FIRST — Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) version 2.0 — The marking system that says who may receive a report: TLP (Traffic Light Protocol):CLEAR, TLP:GREEN, TLP:AMBER, TLP:AMBER+STRICT, TLP:RED. Version 2.0 is authoritative since August 2022. (lesson 3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • MITRE ATT&CK® — The knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Version 20 (October 13, 2026): Enterprise matrix with 15 tactics, 227 techniques and 479 sub-techniques, 178 groups, 842 pieces of software, 57 campaigns. (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • MITRE ATT&CK — Enterprise tactics — The 15 tactics of ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) v20, from Reconnaissance (TA0043) to Impact (TA0040); v20 split the former Defense Evasion tactic into Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112). (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • MITRE ATT&CK — Updates, October 2026 (v20) — The release notes of the current version: new AI-related techniques, new campaigns, detection strategies and analytics. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ATT&CK T1566.004 — Phishing: Spearphishing Voice — The technique that describes the help-desk voice phishing campaign of AL26-028 (Initial Access). (lesson 2,3,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ATT&CK T1190 — Exploit Public-Facing Application — The technique behind the PHP and plugin vulnerabilities on Kalmia's web shop (Initial Access). (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ATT&CK T1078 — Valid Accounts — Use of legitimate credentials — the technique of INC-04 (the former supervisor's account) and of credential-stuffing attacks. (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ATT&CK T1486 — Data Encrypted for Impact — Ransomware encryption (Impact); the event that threatens NAS-01 and its always-connected backup disk. (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ATT&CK T1657 — Financial Theft — Business e-mail compromise and payment fraud (Impact) — the technique of INC-02. (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • MITRE ATT&CK Navigator — A free web tool that colours the techniques you select on the matrix; used in Lab 2 to draw Kalmia's technique heat map. (lesson 2,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments — The method of this course: Task 2-1 (identify threat sources) and Task 2-2 (identify threat events); Appendix D (threat sources, capability/intent/targeting scales) and Appendix E (threat events). Published September 2012, still the final version. (lesson 3,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing — How organizations consume and share threat information: sources, quality of information, handling rules. Background for Lessons 1 and 3. (lesson 1,3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST Computer Security Resource Center — Glossary — The definitions of threat, threat source, threat event, vulnerability, risk and indicator used in this course. (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks — The international standard whose Annex A gives examples of threats and of risk sources; it complements NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-30 in the Integrative Project. (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • NATO AJP-2.1 and the Admiralty (NATO) grading system — US Army FM 2-22.3, Appendix B — The public reproduction of the two scales used in Lesson 3: source reliability A–F and information credibility 1–6. (lesson 3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ODNI Intelligence Community Directive 203 — Analytic Standards — The standard that separates facts from assessments and defines how confidence levels and estimative words are expressed; the Cyber Centre's estimative table follows the same logic. (lesson 3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Microsoft Security Response Center — Security Update Guide — Microsoft's advisories and monthly 'Patch Tuesday' releases (second Tuesday of the month — November 10, 2026 is the next one); the source for Kalmia's Windows and Microsoft 365 assets. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Microsoft — Windows 10 end of support — Windows 10 support ended on October 14, 2025; the consumer Extended Security Updates year ended on October 13, 2026. ROAST-PC and the two sales laptops are affected. (lesson 1,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • WordPress — Security releases (news) — The official announcements of WordPress core security releases; plugin advisories come from the plugin vendors and from CNAs such as Wordfence and Patchstack. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Wordfence Intelligence — WordPress vulnerability database — A CNA that published 3,451 CVEs in 2025, most of them for WordPress plugins; the source of CVE-2026-10795 (UpdraftPlus). (lesson 1,2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • PHP project — security advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618) — The vendor advisory referenced by the CVE record and by AL26-026 — the primary source for the fixed versions. (lesson 2,3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Center for Internet Security — MS-ISAC advisories — Vendor-neutral advisories written for small public-sector and SMB (small and medium-sized business) audiences; a good model of the 'what to do' section of an advisory. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • SANS NewsBites — A twice-weekly e-mail digest of the week's security news with short editor comments — an example of a cyberthreat newsletter. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • SANS Internet Storm Center — Daily diaries and the short daily StormCast podcast written by volunteer handlers; a free, practical daily source. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report — Published May 19, 2026: more than 22,000 confirmed breaches in 145 countries; vulnerability exploitation became the top initial access vector (31 %), ransomware was present in 48 % of breaches and 48 % of breaches involved a third party. (lesson 1,2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Mandiant M-Trends 2026 (Google Cloud) — Annual incident-response report (March 2026): voice phishing became the second most common initial infection vector, with help-desk impersonation used for account takeover. (lesson 1,3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • ENISA Threat Landscape — The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity's annual report on threat trends — a strategic source comparable to the NCTA (National Cyber Threat Assessment). (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • MISP — open-source threat intelligence platform — Free software used by CSIRTs (computer security incident response team) to store and share indicators and reports; an alternative to a spreadsheet for a larger catalogue. (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • OpenCTI — open-source threat intelligence platform — Free platform that models reports, threat actors, techniques (ATT&CK) and the Admiralty reliability/credibility scales natively. (lesson 3,4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • OASIS — STIX 2.1 and TAXII 2.1 standards — The machine-readable format (STIX [Structured Threat Information Expression]) and transport (TAXII [Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information]) used to exchange threat information between platforms and feeds. (lesson 1,3 · check on VirusTotal)
  • VirusTotal — The free multi-engine scanner the Legal Notice (section 14.2 and Annex C) asks you to use on every link and file before opening it. (lesson all · check on VirusTotal)
  • Google Safe Browsing — site status — The second check of Annex C for a domain. (lesson all · check on VirusTotal)
  • Dawson College — Omnivox / Léa — Where Lab 1 (tonight) and Lab 2 (November 14) are submitted: the Lab drop box in Léa. (lesson all · check on VirusTotal)
  • BAnQ — free account for O'Reilly and LinkedIn Learning — Required reading access of the course outline. (lesson all · check on VirusTotal)
  • Python — downloads (3.15.1, October 21, 2026) — The interpreter for code example 4 and for the Lab 2 checker. (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • PowerShell 7.6 (LTS) — install on Windows, Linux and macOS — PowerShell 7.6 LTS (March 18, 2026) runs code example 2 on any platform; Windows PowerShell 5.1 also runs it. (lesson 2 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Git for Windows (Git Bash) — Gives Windows users the Bash shell needed for code example 1; macOS and Linux have Bash already. (lesson 1 · check on VirusTotal)
  • LibreOffice 26.8 — free office suite — LibreOffice Calc opens the Lab 2 workbook if you do not have Microsoft Excel (26.8 released August 26, 2026; 26.2.6 is the enterprise branch). (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • diagrams.net (draw.io) — Free diagram editor used for the infrastructure map in Lab 1 and optional for the catalogue overview in Lab 2. (lesson 4 · check on VirusTotal)
  • Criminal Code of Canada, s. 342.1 (unauthorized use of computer) — statute cited in section 8 of the Legal Notice; applies to any unauthorized access, interception or interference, whatever the intent. (legal · check on VirusTotal)
  • 18 U.S.C. § 1030 — Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (United States) — statute cited in section 8 of the Legal Notice; applies to any unauthorized access, interception or interference, whatever the intent. (legal · check on VirusTotal)
  • Directive 2013/40/EU on attacks against information systems (European Union) — statute cited in section 8 of the Legal Notice; applies to any unauthorized access, interception or interference, whatever the intent. (legal · check on VirusTotal)
  • Ley Orgánica 10/1995, del Código Penal (Spain) — statute cited in section 8 of the Legal Notice; applies to any unauthorized access, interception or interference, whatever the intent. (legal · check on VirusTotal)
